I think it's a good headline. This guy certainly knew that he was placing his wife in fear with his "art." The guy is an abusive troll.

The Court said, in a 7-2 decision, that internet trolling is not enough to establish "specific intent" to meet the mens rea (intent) standard required generally in criminal laws. They said there should be a "true threat" -- a deliberate intention by the speaker to carry out action against his wife -- not just her actual fear. No true threat was shown.

I agree with the Court. I think he has the right to promote his disgusting fantasies as art. But he is definitely an internet troll. It is up to us, the population at large, to support this trolling or oppose it. I oppose it. It is not up to a court to lock him away for it.

Let's do our job now and shun internet trolls.

Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas disagreed. They wanted the court to decide all of the exact details of the intent requirement -- legislating from the bench.

One more thing: this case goes back 'down' for further action on whether there is specific intent in this case. My guess is that they won't find it.

Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas along with Antonin Scalia would have upheld the Stolen Valor Act -- the law that made it a federal crime for anyone to lie about receiving a Congressional Medal of Honor -- even where an old man tells it to his grandson in their living room for the purpose of instilling love of America. Fortunately, in that case, 6 Justices disagreed, and the first-even federal law to ban generalized lying was overturned.
